claims.statement: `backend/mc-service` is the sole authority for movie-collection domain logic: the BFF proxies every client request to it (forwarding the caller's JWT), it persists to its own dedicated MongoDB database `mc_db`, and it validates JWTs locally against a Keycloak JWKS cached at startup rather than calling Keycloak per request.

mc-service startup is a fixed fail-fast sequence: JSON tracing subscriber, `Config::from_env()` requiring `MC_DB_URL`, `KEYCLOAK_URL`, `KEYCLOAK_REALM`, `KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID` and a parseable `MC_SERVICE_PORT` (loading `.env.local` then `.env`), MongoDB connect, idempotent index creation, a read-only orphaned-movies `$lookup` warning check, router build, then `axum::serve` on `0.0.0.0:{MC_SERVICE_PORT}`. A missing variable, an unreachable database, or an unreachable Keycloak JWKS endpoint aborts startup rather than degrading.

mc-service exposes exactly two sub-routers: a public one with unauthenticated `GET /health` and `GET /metrics`, and a `protected` one nested at `/api/v1` carrying every business route (`/collections`, `/collections/{id}`, `/collections/{id}/movies`, `/collections/{id}/movies/filter-options`, `/collections/{id}/movies/count`, `/collections/{id}/movies/{movieId}`, `/movie-metadata`) behind `KeycloakAuthLayer<Role>` plus `require_app_role`.

The literal routes `/collections/{id}/movies/filter-options` and `/collections/{id}/movies/count` are registered BEFORE `/collections/{id}/movies/{movieId}` deliberately, because in the reversed order the parameterised route would shadow them.

Authorization at mc-service is centralized in a Tower layer on the `protected` sub-router: `KeycloakAuthLayer<Role>` is configured with `PassthroughMode::Block`, `persist_raw_claims(false)` and `expected_audiences` set from `KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_ID`, and a separate `require_app_role` middleware applied inside it enforces the OR-logic `mc-user` OR `mc-admin` check (the layer's own `required_roles` is AND-logic and cannot express it). Per-handler `Extension<KeycloakToken<Role>>` extractors only read already-validated claims and must never be the primary guard.

Per-collection DAC is enforced in the application layer by the shared `authorize_collection_access` helper, which every movie command and query calls first: it loads the parent collection, applies the role hierarchy owner ⊇ contributor ⊇ viewer, and reports both a missing collection and an unauthorized caller as `DomainError::CollectionNotFound` (HTTP 404) so the API never leaks whether a collection exists.

A collection's ACL is seeded at creation with exactly one entry, `{ userId: ownerId, role: owner }`; the authorization seam is exercised by the product and by tests, but no UI or endpoint to grant or revoke a contributor/viewer entry exists yet, so every real collection today has only its owner entry.

mc-service is organized into four Clean Architecture layers under a strict outer-to-inner import rule (`src/domain/` never imports from `application`, `adapters` or `api`): domain (entities, `DomainError`, specifications), application (commands, queries, repository trait ports, DTOs, DAC helper), adapters (`src/adapters/mongodb/` repository implementations, BSON↔domain DAOs, indexes) and api (Axum handlers, middleware, router assembly, `AppState`).

mc-service follows CQRS with one file per command (`application/commands/`) and per query (`application/queries/`), each defining its own command/query struct and handler. Handlers depend only on repository trait objects (`Arc<dyn CollectionRepository>`, `Arc<dyn MovieRepository>`) and never the concrete Mongo adapter — the property that makes them unit-testable with `mockall`.

Business-rule validation uses the Specification pattern: `domain/specifications/spec.rs` defines a generic `Specification<T>` trait (`is_satisfied_by`) with `AndSpec`, `OrSpec` and `NotSpec` combinators, and concrete rules are evaluated by command handlers in the application layer before the repository is touched — validation is not delegated to the database.

Handler wiring is direct and has no mediator crate in the request path: `router::build()` constructs the concrete Mongo repositories, coerces them to `Arc<dyn Trait>` trait objects, builds one handler per operation, packs them all into a single `AppState` injected as `State<Arc<AppState>>`, and Axum handlers call the matching `AppState` field's `handle()` method. (`docs/MCM-Architecture.md`'s "CQRS via `medi-rs`" phrasing describes the intent, not the shipped dispatch.)

mc-service maps typed `DomainError` variants to RFC 9457 `application/problem+json` responses through the API-layer `problem_response` / `domain_error_to_response` helpers, never a stack trace; the `type` field is a non-resolvable `.example` namespace URI and `detail` is a fixed per-variant client-safe message while internal detail is logged server-side only.

Cascade delete of a collection and its movies runs inside one MongoDB multi-document transaction in `MongoCollectionRepository::delete()`, so mc-service requires a replica-set-enabled MongoDB (a bare standalone `mongod` cannot serve it); a misconfigured single-member replica set that advertises an internal-only hostname also breaks host-side tests.

The dev mc-service MongoDB service is started with `--wiredTigerCacheSizeGB 1` plus `--setParameter wiredTigerFileHandleCloseIdleTime=30 --setParameter wiredTigerFileHandleCloseMinimum=250` (MongoDB's own WiredTiger sweeper defaults) to stop the heap growth that OOM-killed mongod mid-run: with MongoDB's raised thresholds (`closeIdleTime=600 s`, `closeMinimum=2000`) nothing was ever eligible for sweeping, so data handles reached 65,844 for 2 live collections. These WiredTiger parameters are startup-only — `setParameter` at runtime is refused — and `compose.prod.yaml` carries its own `command` and is unaffected.

The mc-service integration harness no longer mints a unique database per test: `common::test_db()` leases a bounded pool slot named `mc_test_s<slot>` (≤64 slots, tracked in the `mc_test_pool.leases` collection), resets the leased database on ACQUIRE rather than on release, and `cleanup_db` is a deliberate no-op. Cleaning on acquire is what makes a panicking test harmless, since a test that dies never reaches its own cleanup; `tests/integration/pool_test.rs` exists to pin the pool properties a green suite cannot show.

`nx test mc-service` and `nx test:integration mc-service` now run the integration binaries identically: the `test` target declares `dependsOn: [test:unit, test:integration]` and executes no cargo of its own, so `--test-threads=1` is decided in exactly one place — `scripts/mc-service-integration-guard.mjs`. This reconciliation exists because a developer-facing `nx test` at default parallelism disagreed with the CI gate, hiding a flake that failed ~2 runs in 3 locally while staying green in CI for months. Measured after the fix, from a clean MongoDB: 2 failures in 29 runs at default parallelism (always in `movies::large_collection_test`, as an index-creation failure or a `MovieNotFound` read-your-own-writes miss), versus 180/180 serial — so the pin must not be flipped to parallel without first fixing the contention.

The fast Rust gate's clippy run uses `--all-targets -- -D warnings`, with the `--all-targets` flag placed before the bare `--`; without it clippy checks lib and bins only and nothing in the fast `mc-service-checks` job compiles `backend/mc-service/tests/**`, which is how a pull request once went green while all three integration test binaries failed to compile.

mc-service's low unit-only coverage (~29%) is by design, not a gap: Clean Architecture pushes the MongoDB adapter and Axum API layers behind integration tests, and the enforced ≥70% line-coverage floor is measured over unit + integration together with `cargo tarpaulin --manifest-path backend/mc-service/Cargo.toml --ignore-tests --out Lcov`. `cargo-tarpaulin` is a dev dependency of the crate, not a standalone install.

The vendored OpenSSL dependency is gated behind `[target.'cfg(target_env = "musl")'.dependencies]` in `Cargo.toml` because the Alpine/musl Docker build needs statically linked OpenSSL that Alpine's `openssl-dev` does not ship; moving it into the unconditional `[dependencies]` section silently breaks `cargo test` on Windows, where `perl` (required to build OpenSSL from source) is absent.

Because Keycloak JWKS/discovery is fetched once inside a `tokio::spawn` at router construction, integration tests must await the auth instance reaching operational state before the first request rather than merely yielding: `common::build_test_app_inner()` gates on `wait_until_operational()` (success, not just a completed attempt) and panics on timeout. A failed discovery still flips the instance to "ready", so without that gate the whole auth-negative suite would pass green against a dead Keycloak.

`/metrics` remains usable when the router is built repeatedly in one process: `router::build()` attempts to install a global Prometheus recorder and, if one is already installed (the integration-test case), falls back to building an isolated recorder whose handle still renders valid Prometheus text, so the endpoint returns 200 rather than panicking.

mc-service ships as an Alpine/musl container built in a two-stage Dockerfile: the build stage installs `musl-dev perl make` and compiles the release binary, and the runtime stage installs only `ca-certificates tzdata`, copies the statically linked binary, runs it as the non-root user `mcservice`, and exposes port 3001.

On startup mc-service runs a read-only orphan check: a `$lookup` aggregate against `movie_collections` matching movies whose parent collection is missing, which only emits `tracing::warn!` with the count (or an info log when zero) and never modifies data; aggregate or cursor failures downgrade to a warning as well.
